AEP20806.name: Institutional Economics and Economic Organisation Theory

descriptions.AK: DEC10306 Economics; UEC10406 Microeconomics and Behaviour.
descriptions.CO: The course has been completely revised compared with previous years. The renewed course engages you with economic, business and political actuality by means of weekly case studies. Using six weekly case studies, you will deepen your understanding of both the cases themselves and the theories of institutional economics and economic organisation. The cases address contemporary issues in the political and economic landscape, including futures markets, real estate development, land tenure, and alternative food supply chains. They cover examples from both Western and non-Western countries. So, through the case studies, you will gain insight into the cases discussed and develop the ability to analyse and conceptualise real-world economic situations and policy dilemmas. Institutional economics and economic organisation theory extend beyond traditional economic theories by placing human behaviour, individual characteristics, and institutional constraints at the centre of the analysis. They help explain why different organisational forms emerge to provide the goods and services we consume, how governments can design effective policies to encourage or discourage certain behaviours, and why firms and countries adopt different institutional arrangements and policy approaches.
descriptions.AC: attending lectures and studying the book; working on problem sets / doing exercises; presenting in class and discussing; writing assignments.
descriptions.LT: Required reading /literature: see course guide. The course is supported by a Brightspace site.

objectives: Describe the causes and effects of transaction costs
Apply institutional and economic organisation theories
Interpret coordination and motivation mechanisms
Analyse the behaviour of individuals and organisations

AEP21306.name: Econometrics

descriptions.AK: YSS20306 Quantitative and Qualitative Research Techniques in the Social Sciences; MAT20306 Advanced Statistics; MAT22306 Quantitative Research Methodology and Statistics.
descriptions.CO: Social scientists are often interested in relationships between different variables, e.g. consumption and prices. The objective of econometrics is to quantify such relationships using available data and statistical techniques and to interpret and use the resulting outcomes. So, econometrics is the interaction between (economic) theory, data and statistical methods (e.g. estimation and testing). The interaction of these three elements makes econometrics interesting and a must for the dedicated social scientist. The use of econometric tools stretches from economic and business disciplines to social science fields like sociology and history. The course helps to understand a number of econometric issues and techniques, where emphasis is on applying econometrics to research questions in the broad field of social sciences.
descriptions.AC: - attending lectures and studying the textbook; - attending practical sessions doing exercises and discussing the outcomes; - attending computer practicals to work on exercises using econometric software (STATA).
descriptions.LT: Course guide available in Brightspace. Handbook: C. Dougherty (2016). Introduction to Econometrics. 5th ed. Oxford University Press.

objectives: Compare various econometric techniques
Interpret econometric models and results of analysis
Calculate econometric tests statistics and indicators
Assess the quality of econometric analyses on the basis of various statistical tests and indicators
Construct simple econometric models and estimate them using econometric techniques

AEP21806.name: The Economics of Agriculture, Food and Policy

descriptions.AK: UEC10406 Microeconomics and Behaviour; DEC21806 Macroeconomics and International Trade
descriptions.CO: The course 'The Economics of Agriculture, Food and Policy' gives an introduction to (mainly EU) agri-food policies and the analysis of their economic effects. Issues dealt with are the history and motives of EU agri-food policies; policy instruments frequently used at global scale and their effects on domestic and international food trade and markets as well as developing countries. Moreover, AEP21806 deals with the Common Agricultural Policy of the EU and its problems and reforms and core aspects of international agricultural trade negotiations. Also the relationships between agri-food policies and rural development, the environment, animal welfare, and food safety are discussed.
descriptions.AC: The course consists of lectures, practicals, preparing short presentations and the writing of a policy brief. Students compete with each other in government groups playing the simulation game AGRIPOL. AGRIPOL quantifies the complex effects of agri-food policy choices on food markets and national welfare of individual countries as well as the entire world. Students apply policy instruments and learn by own experience to what effects and international complications national policy decisions may lead. During the practicals, the (unforeseeable) effects of various policy changes are analysed in detail. In the policy brief, students analyse and reflect on one chosen agri-food policy problem in detail. In the presentations, students analyse their country’s food market and their policy decisions.
descriptions.LT: Obligatory reading: manual and backgrounder of the AGRIPOL game as well as the policy brief guidelines. Recommended book covering most topics of the lecture: Oskam, Meester, Silvis (2011). EU policy for agriculture, food and rural areas. Wageningen Academic Publishers. Additional facultative reading: A list of suggested readings for each lecture will be made available in Brightspace in the section ‘Course Documents/ Suggested reading and further literature hints’. A study collection of further reading on agricultural policies and agricultural economics will be available in the Leeuwenborch library during the duration of the course (ask at the library reception for it). The collection provides several textbooks which can be useful for deepening the contents of the course.

objectives: Explain the evolution, motives, design and problems of agri-food policies in the EU (LO1)
Analyse national and international impacts that agricultural policy instruments have on different stakeholders (LO2)
Understand and analyse major economic aspects of the design, implementation and evaluation of agri-food policies (LO3)
Understand public and political debates on agricultural policy issues and to be able to reflect on these issues her- or himself (LO4)
Apply the theoretical knowledge on the links between economic analysis and agro-food policies gained during the course to a real-world problem (LO5)

AEP31806.name: Industrial Organization

descriptions.AK: Microeconomics, Mathematics at the level of MAT14803 Mathematics 1, AEP33306 (Economics of Agribusiness)
descriptions.CO: This course is part of the study programs BEB Economics and Governance (compulsory). It could also be attractive to BBC and MME Business programmes. Students are expected to be comfortable with basic algebra and calculus, including systems of equations, derivatives, logarithms, and NPV calculations. Knowledge of microeconomics at the level of Microeconomics (DEC21806 Microeconomics) or Economics of Agribusiness (AEP33306 – for BBC and MME Business programmes) is a prerequisite. The central questions addressed by industrial organization are: (i) Is there market power? (ii) How do firms acquire and maintain market power? (iii) What are the implications of market power? (iv) Is there a role for public policy with regard to market power? This course takes a formal approach to analyzing the way firms make production and sales decisions and interact strategically with each other in the marketplace. Whereas microeconomics typically focuses on the extreme cases of monopoly and perfect competition, industrial organization is primarily concerned with the intermediate case of oligopoly, that is, competition between a few firms (more than one, as in monopoly, but not as many as in competitive markets). We will cover selected topics of industrial organization, including price discrimination, oligopoly, collusion and price wars, market structure, horizontal mergers, and vertical relations. We will illustrate these issues by using examples from agriculture and other sectors. Readings in the textbook will provide background and introduction to a variety of topics, many of which will be covered in class in greater depth. Exercises solved in class and problem sets will focus on formal analysis. Supplemental readings will provide additional motivation and opportunities to develop intuition.
descriptions.AC: - attending lectures and studying the materials; - attending practical sessions with analytical exercises; - writing a research proposal.
descriptions.LT: Book: Luís M. B. Cabral (2017). Introduction to Industrial Organization (Second edition). The MIT Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts (available in the library and at https://wurreadershop.proefschriftmaken.nl/shop/wur. Other study material: Available on Brightspace for this course. If you have any questions, contact your course coordinator.
descriptions.CON: Dr. Dušan Drabik (coordinator), tel. 0317 484365; C2105 Leeuwenborch

objectives: Provide at least four classes of problems industrial organisation deals with
Independently solve and interpret the results of exercises similar to the solved exercises provided in the course
Approach and analyse the type of industrial organisational problems covered in the course
Explain intuitively economic phenomena in the area of industrial organisation

DEC10306.name: Economics

descriptions.CC: DEC23806 Microeconomics for Development DEC23306 Intermediate Microeconomics DEC20806 Introduction to Development Economics
descriptions.CO: The economics discipline has made great strides in developing tools that can help us understand, explain, and address the challenges currently facing our world. This introductory economics course introduces key tools and concepts such as strategic interaction (game theory), limited information, principal–agent models, human behaviors and preferences, including not only self-interest and risk aversion but also altruism, as well as dynamic processes of change such as creative destruction and instability. Standard tools are taught by showing how they give insight into real-world problems such as inequality and sustainability. The course makes extensive use of data and cutting-edge empirical research. The course teaches students how economists work: Start with a question, and look at the evidence. Build a model that helps understand what you see. Critically evaluate the model: does it provide insight into the question and explain the evidence?
descriptions.AC: lectures, tutorials, and group assignments
descriptions.LT: The Economy 2.0: Microeconomics, available at https://core-econ.org/the-economy, the App Store or Google Play.

objectives: Understand basic economic theories related to decision making of consumers and firms and its consequences for society
Apply game theory to analyse simple societal dilemmas
Explain how differences in endowments and power relations shape patterns of inequality and sustainability
Apply graphs and calculus to solve constrained choice problems
Critically appraise economic theory with real-world evidence

DEC21806.name: Macroeconomics and International Trade

descriptions.AK: DEC10306 Economics; DEC23806 Microeconomics for Development UEC10406 Microeconomics and Behaviour.
descriptions.CC: AEP30306 The Economics of European Integration: Agricultural, Rural and Regional Policy Analysis; DEC32306 International Economics: Trade and Development; DEC30306 Central Themes in Economics of Development.
descriptions.CO: Assuming a basic knowledge of economics, the present course deepens one's understanding of the closed economy and extends the analysis to an open economy. It explains things like inflation, unemployment, current account deficits, international debt, and depreciating exchange rates, and also pays attention to the role of economic policy instruments. In addition, it reviews the theories that explain international trade patterns between countries and also international movements of production factors. Further, it studies the effects of different kinds of trade protection like tariffs and quotas and also pays attention to political aspects of trade policy.
descriptions.AC: Lectures on the course materials. Practicals in which students make exercises on the course materials, and use quantitative information about country differences in macroeconomic and international trade conditions and policies.
descriptions.LT: The course material consists of two books: - Krugman, P.R., M. Obstfeld, M.J. Melitz, International Economics. Theory and Policy, 12th edition, Addison-Wesley, 2021; - Mankiw, N.G. , Macroeconomics, 12th edition, Worth Publishers, 2025.

objectives: Apply the basic concepts of open-economy macroeconomics and international economics
Apply the trade theories based on comparative advantage and scale economies
Identify the gains of trade and its income distribution effects
Analyse the effects of international factor mobility
Analyse the income distribution effects of trade instruments
Construct (in a conceptual way) the current account and the balance of payments
Apply both the Keynesian model and the Classical model for an open economy
Analyse the effects of fiscal, monetary, and trade policies in both the short and the long run
Understand the basics of the money market and the market of foreign exchange

DEC23306.name: Intermediate Microeconomics

descriptions.AK: MAT12806 Mathematics M (Mathematics for Social Sciences) or MAT14803 Mathematics 1; ECH10406 Microeconomics and Behaviour or DEC10306 Economics
descriptions.CC: ENR22306 Public Sector Economics; ENR21806 Environmental Economics in Practice; UEC22806 Spatial and Regional Economics; AEP20806 Institutional Economics and Economic Organisation Theory; AEP21806 Agriculture Food and Policy; DEC32306 International Economics: Trade and Development; ECH32306 Advanced Microeconomics; DEC30306 Central Themes in Economics of Development
descriptions.CO: This course aims to develop students’ analytic approach to, as well as deepen their understanding of, the foundational concepts of microeconomics. It covers consumer and producer theory in-depth and builds up to the analysis of markets. The course will enable students to translate core microeconomic phenomenon into mathematical models, to solve these mathematical models using computation and and graphical tools, and to use these models to analyze the the impact of relevant government policy. It also extends models of microeconomic behavior to cover aspects like behavior under uncertainty, issues of asymmetric information, and market failures.
descriptions.AC: Lectures, tutorials, and self-study.
descriptions.LT: Varian, H. Intermediate Microeconomics. (2014). Norton & Company, New York. (9th International student edition). Bergstrom, T.C.; Varian, H.R. (2014). Workout in Intermediate Microeconomics. Norton & Company, New York. (9th edition).

objectives: Translate socioeconomic phenomenon at the consumer and producer level into mathematical microeconomic models
Solve these microeconomic models to analyse consumer, producer, and market behavior
Utilise a combination of mathematical, computational, and graphical tools for economic analysis
Apply microeconomic theory and analysis to predict the effects of government policy on individuals and markets
Apply microeconomic theory and analysis to issues of market failure and government intervention
Extend microeconomic models to incorporate aspects like behavior under uncertainty and asymmetric information

DEC24303.name: Economic Growth and Development

descriptions.AK: DEC21806 Macroeconomics and International Trade.
descriptions.CO: Note: This course will be offered in 2027-2028 for the first time. Why are some countries rich while others remain poor? Why do economies grow at different rates, and what explains the large and persistent differences in living standards across the world? These questions lie at the heart of economic growth and development and form the central focus of this course. The course provides an in-depth introduction to the theory and empirics of long-run economic growth, with particular attention to the determinants of cross-country differences in income, productivity, and welfare. The course combines theoretical models with empirical analysis to examine the principal drivers of economic growth and development. These include physical and human capital accumulation, population dynamics, technological progress, innovation, institutional quality, geography, natural resources, and international economic integration. Throughout the course, theoretical predictions are confronted with real-world evidence, allowing students to assess why some countries have achieved sustained increases in productivity and living standards while others have experienced stagnation, recurrent growth reversals, or persistent poverty.
descriptions.AC: lectures; assignment.
descriptions.LT: Jones, C. en Vollrath, D. Introduction to Economic Growth . 4e editie. W.W. Norton & Company Een aantal aanvullende wetenschappelijke artikelen.

objectives: Describe the central concepts, empirical facts, models, and determinants of economic growth, and clearly interpret income differences between countries.
Empirically measure economic productivity and growth patterns using international datasets such as the Penn World Tables.
Conduct growth accounting to identify and quantify the sources of economic growth.
Analyse and apply the Solow growth model and endogenous growth models to straightforward economic problems.
Analyse the effect of capital accumulation, population growth, human capital, and technological development on economic growth.
Critically assess how geographical factors, natural resources, institutional quality, and policy affect economic growth.
Apply theoretical models to analyse the growth performance of a specific country and formulate well-founded policy recommendations.

DEC32306.name: International Economics: Trade and Development

descriptions.AK: DEC21806 Macroeconomics and International Trade; DEC23306 Intermediate Microeconomics or AEP20306 Economics of Agribusiness; AEP21306 Econometrics
descriptions.CC: BEB Thesis; DEC-30306 Central Themes in Economics of Development
descriptions.CO: This course focuses on the impacts of globalization and trade policies in developing countries. Topics covered include effects of international trade on inequality and productivity, impacts of health and safety standards on developing countries, and impacts of strategic trade competition between major powers on developing countries, among others. The theoretical models pertaining to these issues are discussed, building on microeconomics and on standard trade models. Recent empirical evidence will also be covered. Through assignments, discussions, and an individual paper, students will address some of the most important current issues related to international trade and development.
descriptions.AC: Lectures, tutorials, group work, and an individual paper.
descriptions.LT: Recent academic articles, these will be made available through Brightspace.

objectives: Analyse recent empirical trends in globalisation and international trade flows
Identify the channels through which international trade affects people and firms in developing countries
Understand and apply the main economic theories on the effects of international trade on wages, poverty, inequality, and productivity in developing countries
Analyse the implications of trade standards with respect to labor and food
Critically review empirical literature on the impacts of international trade in developing countries
Analyse the most important consequences of the strategic trade competition between major powers (US, China, EU) for developing countries

ENP30306.name: International Environmental Policy

descriptions.AK: Students are expected to have basic knowledge about core concepts and principles of environmental policy, for instance obtained from courses like ENP34306 Environmental Policy: Analysis and Evaluation and YES30806 Environmental Quality and Governance.
descriptions.CC: ENP39306 Advanced International Environmental Politics and Diplomacy ENP80424/36 Thesis Environmental Policy
descriptions.CO: The course introduces students to the world of international environmental policy and provides them with concepts and methods to analyze and understand a variety of international environmental regimes. Students will go beyond knowing that there is such a thing as international environmental policy and that it faces many problems, to understanding what these problems are and how the actors involved try to address them. The course takes place in the form of alternating theory and case-study lectures, with a weekly tutorial focused on enhancing practical analytical skills. It provides students with an analytical toolbox to assess the structure and effectiveness of an international environmental regime, helping students to simplify the complex world of international environmental policy for purposes of analysis. Students will learn how to identify and formulate pertinent research questions in this field. Their acquired knowledge will be assessed in the form of a group-poster, an individual essay and a written exam.
descriptions.AC: theory readings and lectures; case study readings and lectures; practical tutorials; individual essay; written exam.
descriptions.LT: Is made available in Brightspace.

objectives: Explain the meaning and relevance of key concepts in international environmental policy
Make use of conceptual frameworks from international relations and global governance
Analyse the structure and dynamics of an international environmental regime
Visualise the main elements and relationships of an international environmental regime
Write clearly and concisely to effectively formulate and defend an own viewpoint

ENR20306.name: Environmental Economics and Environmental Policy

descriptions.AK: An introduction course in economics (e.g. DEC10306 Economics) and knowledge of basic calculus (e.g. MAT14803 Mathematics 1).
descriptions.CC: ENR21806 Environmental Economics in Practice; ENP30306 International Environmental Policy.
descriptions.CO: The main aim of the course is to gain insights into environmental problems from an economic and policy point of view. The course provides an introduction into environmental economics and environmental policy and their application. The central theme is the relationship between society, the economy, and the environment, with application to various themes (e.g. biodiversity conservation, climate change, plastic pollution). We will analyse the mechanisms behind causes of environmental degradation, as well as the effectiveness and efficiency of policy instruments. Problems will be analysed on multiple scales, reaching from the global to local level. During the course, the responsibilities and roles of different actors will be discussed and how they can form obstacles or windows of opportunity for implementing environmental policies. Furthermore, theoretical insights will be applied to contemporary environmental problems.
descriptions.AC: Students prepare the literature that will be discussed during the lectures. During tutorials, students apply methods and theories discussed during the lectures on applied problems. Furthermore, students will work in groups to analyse the drivers and trends of an important environmental problem, as well as potential policy solutions.
descriptions.LT: Literature will be announced at a later stage.

objectives: Explain the relation between the environment, society and the economy in the context of environmental problems and sustainability issues
Apply basic theories and tools from economics and policy science to causes and potential solutions of environmental problems
Evaluate the performance of different economic and policy instruments in environmental policies
Discuss the responsibilities for environmental problems at different scales and from different actor perspectives
Evaluate the performance and integration of different policy instruments to solve environmental problems
Analyse a contemporary environmental problem in a specific context using insights from economic and policy theories

ENR21806.name: Environmental Economics in Practice

descriptions.AK: ENR34306 Environmental Economics for Environmental Sciences or ENR20306 Environmental Economics and Policy.
descriptions.CC: BSc Thesis Environmental Economics and Natural Resources
descriptions.CO: This course prepares BSc students for a BSc thesis at the ENR group. Students are introduced to the core themes of the ENR group: climate change, social-ecological systems, and environmental-economic behavioural choices. Each theme is dealt with in lectures on the economic theory of the topic and in tutorials or computer practical to practice a quantitative analysis tool for this topic, such as bioeconomic models, statistical analysis, or cost-benefit analysis. In addition students write a literature review on a topic of their own choice, which may or may not be related to any of the three core themes of ENR.
descriptions.AC: The core themes climate change, social-ecological systems, and environmental-economic behavioural choices are discussed in a theory part and a practice part. The theory part consists of reading material, online knowledge clips, and discussion lectures. The discussion lectures will build on, rather than summarize, the course material so students are expected to prepare for the discussion lecture by studying the reading material and watching the knowledge clips. Reading questions are offered to guide students through the course material, and quizzes to enable students to test their understanding. The practice part entails tutorials with quantitative economic analysis tools. In addition to the lectures and tutorials, students will write a literature review about the economic and environmental literature on a topic of the student's own choice. This could be one of the three themes discussed in the lectures, but students are free to choose another topic. The literature review will be discussed in tutorials where students can compare each other's review and get feedback from their peers and lecturers.
descriptions.LT: Literature for this course will consist of selected reports and scientific articles on the topics selected for the course. The literature, or the references to the literature, will be provided through Brightspace.

objectives: Explain for the core ENR themes what economic mechanisms underlie these problems and how they might be analysed
Apply basic quantitative economic analysis tools to analyse environmental problems
Write a literature review on an environmental-economic topic of their own choice
Explain the different steps in a cost-benefit analysis and its role in the process of environmental policy-making

ENR22306.name: Public Sector Economics

descriptions.AK: UEC10406 Microeconomics and Behaviour; DEC23306 Intermediate Microeconomics; and MAT14803 Mathematics Applied: Introduction (or any equivalent calculus course)
descriptions.CO: This course considers the role of the government in the economy. It does so from a microeconomic perspective. The course deals with the taxing and spending activities of the government, the behavioral responses of consumers and firms, and how the government influences the allocation of resources and the distribution of income. The course extensively discusses the actual financial position of the Dutch government, the existing financial norms about government debts and budget deficits, the present organisation of the Dutch social security system, and the relationship with the European Union.
descriptions.AC: The course includes lectures and tutorials. In the lectures we present the main topics and some seminal models of public sector economics. Exercises are scheduled along with the lectures to foster acquaintance with economic models of the public sector. During several tutorials, students discuss current issues of Dutch public policies. Finally, students have to present main insights on the organisation of the Dutch public sector and contemporary Dutch policy.
descriptions.LT: Stiglitz, J.E. and Rosengard, J.K. Economics of the Public Sector. Fourth International Student Edition, 2015. W.W. Norton & Company. ISBN 0393937097. De Kam, Bolhuis en Lukkezen, Overheidsfinanciën, 16e druk, 2021. Noordhoff Uitgevers. Compulsory readings (mandatory for written exam) for lectures on Dutch Public Finance and fiscal federalism; a list will be provided on the Brightspace page of the course.

objectives: Identify relevant market failures, distributional concerns, and the conditions under which government intervention may improve social welfare.
Apply economic models and quantitative tools to analyse public policies, such as taxation, pensions, and social-insurance.
Explain the role of collective decision-making and public institutions in the design and implementation of public policies.
Interpret empirical evidence on public policies.
Develop evidence-based policy recommendations for the Dutch welfare system.

MAT15203.name: Mathematics Applied: Linear Algebra

MAT15303.name: Statistics 1

descriptions.CO: Data collection; descriptive statistics; practical notion of probability; basic probability theory; derivation of the binomial distribution; normal distribution; principles of hypothesis testing; the binomial test and test for a population mean; properties of the mean of a random sample as an estimator of a population mean; basic notion of consistency. Ethical issues, as touching upon good statistical practice, will be discussed in class.

MAT15403.name: Statistics 2

descriptions.CC: MAT20306 Advanced Statistics; MAT22306, MAT24306 Advanced Statistics for Nutritionists.
descriptions.CO: Building on an understanding of (simple) models, implications of model assumptions, interpretation of parameters; checking model assumptions; testing hypotheses for population means, for the 1-sample and 2-samples situations, for independent normal data (t-test); construction of a confidence interval for a population mean, or difference in means; simple linear regression and correlation, estimation, hypothesis testing and construction of a confidence interval for intercept, slope and predictions. Ethical issues, as touching upon good statistical practice, will be discussed in class.
descriptions.AC: tutorials that are motivated by practical problems from the Life Sciences, including making exercises; and (compulsory) computer practicals, analysing practical data with statistical software.
descriptions.LT: R. Lyman Ott; Michael Longnecker. (2013). An introduction to statistical methods and data analysis. 7th edition, ISBN-13: 978-1-305-26947-7 (6th edition may also be used). Lecture notes provide an introduction to tutorials, exercises, and a reading guide for the book and the computer practicals.

Apply a hypothesis test for a (difference of) population mean(s), intercept or slope (t-test)
Construct a confidence interval for a (difference of) population mean(s), intercept, slope and predictions
Show understanding of the implications of model assumptions
Apply checks for model assumptions

MAT20306.name: Advanced Statistics

descriptions.AK: MAT15303 Statistics 1 + MAT15403 Statistics 2 or MAT14303 Basic Statistics or MAT15403 Statistics 2. The student should be familiar with 1) The principles of probability calculus and the subjects: estimation, construction of confidence intervals and hypothesis testing from statistical inference 2) Application of these principles to inference about central values (mean or success probability) for the 1-sample and 2-sample situations, in case of Normal observations and binary (0,1) observations 3) Methods of analysis for simple (one explanatory variable) linear regression. To refresh this knowledge, (parts of) chapters 1 to 6 and 11 of the book can be studied. or the Brightspace Module 'Ready to Advance in Statistics' can be worked through. Via Brightspace > Discover, enroll yourself.
descriptions.CC: Statistics for Data Scientists (MAT32806) Bayesian Data Analysis (MAT34806) Data Science for Plant Breeding and Genetics (MAT33306) Advanced Data Analysis for Agricultural Research (MAT35306)
descriptions.CO: This course covers several more advanced statistical models and associated designs, and techniques for statistical inference, as relevant to life science studies. The main topics are categorical data, (multiple) regression, analysis of variance (including multiple comparisons), analysis of covariance, and non-parametric tests. The aims of an analysis, the model assumptions, the properties (and limitations) of the models and associated inferential techniques and the interpretation of results in terms of the practical problem will be discussed. Focus will be upon students gaining an understanding of the model ingredients, an (intuitive) understanding of inferential techniques, insight into data structures and implications for choice of model and analysis. Students will be able to perform analysis of data with statistical software, i.e. with R-Studio.
descriptions.AC: Per week we will have 2 lectures of two hours each, 2 computer practicals of two hours each and one practical where students will do exercises with pen and paper.- lectures: follow classes; - study the book and make exercises; - computer practicals (compulsory): (learn how to) use R-Studio and PQRS, and work on case studies; - pen and paper practicals: work on exercises and case studies where computer output is given.
descriptions.LT: R. Lyman Ott; Longnecker, M.T. (2016). An Introduction to Statistical Methods and Data Analysis. 7th ed. 1174p. Lecture notes available in English. You can order your readers at https://wurreadershop.proefschriftmaken.nl/shop/wur. For literature books, please go to https://wur.acco.be/ If you have any questions, contact your course coordinator.

objectives: Formulate a statistical hypothesis based on a research question
Recognise a valid experimental design or sampling procedure for data collection
Select an appropriate statistical model that allows valid estimation, quantification of uncertainty, and hypothesis testing given the research question and properties of the data
Produce relevant computer output in R (RStudio) for a given data set and research question
Interpret the outcome of the statistical analysis, draw valid conclusions and argue the relevance for the actual problem

PAP10306.name: Public Administration and Policy Making

descriptions.CC: PAP30806 Governance and policy change; PAP21806 European Union institutions and policies; FNP31806 Social and Political Theory for Forest and Nature Conservation; PAP30306 Designing Innovative Governance Arrangements
descriptions.CO: People expect a lot of 'government' or of 'policy' when it comes to dealing with pressing societal problems like climate change, sustainable agro-food chains, economic reforms or public health services. But what are the possibilities for governmental organisations to intervene in complex societal processes? How do bureaucracies, politics and policymaking in the contemporary network society work? What are the main theories about the organisation and management of public institutions? And what does it mean that public organizations are dependent on companies and citizens who have considerable resources at their disposal, follow their own goals and are not just subject to regulation but try to influence society themselves? This course provides basic knowledge about public institutions and discusses the main themes, concepts and tools of public administration, politics and policy making.
descriptions.AC: interactive lectures based on background reading; tutorials and exercises with public administration tools and instruments; excursion to a governmental organisation application of theoretical and methodological insights in simulated policy game.
descriptions.LT: M.J.W., van den Berg, C.F., van der Steen, M.A. en L.G. Tummers (2021) Openbaar Bestuur: Beleid, organisatie en politiek. 10e herziene druk, Wolters Kluwer Breeman G.E., en C.J.A. van Eijk (2023) De bestuurlijke kaart van Nederland: het openbaar bestuur en zijn omgeving in nationaal en internationaal perspectief, 8e druk, Coutinho: Bussum. 9789046908501

objectives: Acquiring knowledge about the political-administrative institutions and organisations of public administration in a national and international perspective
Gaining knowledge of the key concepts and theories in public administration
Applying these concepts and theories to cases related to the life science domains of Wageningen University
Acquiring knowledge of the main analytical tools in public administration
Applying these analytical tools to cases related to the domains of Wageningen.
Developing insight into the functioning of public administration and cultivating some political-administrative sensitivity

PAP21806.name: European Union Institutions and Policies

descriptions.AK: None, although having followed courses with a PAP-code is an advantage.
descriptions.CC: RHI-52806 The making of Europe and the European Union; for students who are interested in reflecting on Europe from a historical perspective. PAP30806 Governance and Policy Change; for those interested in learning more about public administration and policy theories.
descriptions.CO: Climate change and environmental degradation, thousands of migrants who try to cross the Mediterranean on shaky boats, the return of geopolitical conflicts, vast trade agreements that are being negotiated and simultaneously face strong critiques; for many of today's most pressing crises and challenges, citizens, media, and even national politicians look at the European Union institutions for developing effective solutions. Others, on the contrary, blame the European project for being the main reason why these crises have emerged in the first place. In either case, the European Union has a major influence on setting legal frameworks, particularly also in the life sciences domains. The aim of this course is to make students familiar with the basic principles, institutions and policy processes at the EU-level. The course introduces students to the EU's history, its main institutions and legal frameworks, the policymaking process, and the political struggles that take place around a number of policy domains that are relevant to the life sciences. Although the course is primarily targeted at students of the BSc Economics and Governance (BEB), it is accessible to and insightful for students from different backgrounds who are interested in the basic functioning of the EU and its main policies in the ‘Wageningen domains’. The first half of the course provides a general background to the EU, including its history, main institutions, decision-making procedures, and implementation pathways. In the second half of the course we will discuss the development of a number of relevant policy domains: the internal market, migration policy, marine policy, environmental policy, agricultural policy, and food policy. At the end of the course, students will be able to explain the functioning of the EU’s main institutions and policies, to use and analyze official EU documents and legislation, and to critically appraise an ongoing policy debate. Beside lectures, the course entails an excursion to Brussels, during which students will experience EU policy-making in real-life. In addition, during the whole course students work on a group paper about an ongoing EU policy debate, such as the Common Agricultural Policy, GMOs, the MERCOSUR trade agreement, the distribution of refugees, or the supervision of banks. The course ends with an exam that tests the knowledge obtained.
descriptions.AC: - lectures; - reading literature; - analyzing a case and writing a group paper; - providing feedback on the work of other groups; - excursion.
descriptions.LT: Lieveldt, H. & S. Princen (2023). The Politics of the European Union, 3rd ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. + selection of articles and book chapters.

objectives: Explain the history and functioning of the main EU institutions and policymaking processes
Explain the EU's relevance for the life sciences domains
Retrieve and analyse official EU documents and legislation
Analyse and appraise an ongoing EU policy debate by using a range of key concepts and theories

PAP30306.name: Designing Innovative Governance Arrangements

descriptions.AK: Introduction course: PAP10306 Public Administration and Policy Making or other public administration course.
descriptions.CO: Government, business and civil society can get caught up in societal problems that persist over years, despite the numerous efforts to remedy them. These problems are labeled as 'wicked' and are characterized by both social and technical complexity. Many actors are involved and the issues are hard to pin down. Such a context calls for designing new, innovative governance arrangements. In this course we discuss different designing methods and the underlying governance theories such as collaborative governance and deliberative governance. We will discuss policy design issues at different levels. You will apply these theories and methods by analyzing wicked problem cases and by designing innovative governance arrangements in a realistic case related to your own domain.
descriptions.AC: plenary lectures; practicals; project group meetings.
descriptions.LT: Reader.

objectives: Understand the main aspects of designing steering arrangements, process architecture and interventions
Analyse and translate policy and policy process problems into design questions
Apply and evaluate different design and intervention methods and tools
Design innovative policy arrangements taking into account relevant organisational, institutional and decision-making aspects

PAP30806.name: Governance and Policy Change

descriptions.AK: PAP10306 Public administration and policy making; PAP20306 Studying governance: Key concepts and leading authors; or an alternative introductory course to public administration
descriptions.CC: PAP30306 Designing Innovative Governance Arrangements; PAP40806 Textual Data Science for Comparative Public Governance; PAP21806 European Union Institutions and Policies; PAP21306 International Policies and Institutions; In addition, the Public Administration and Policy group offers a range of thesis and capita selecta opportunities.
descriptions.CO: The classical roles of governments are the provision of public goods and the prevention of negative external effects. However, the call for more and different kinds of policy interventions has become louder. Politicians and citizens demand new types of authorities to control markets, better monitoring systems, and intelligent regulations. These calls are accompanied by new forms of arrangements between government, private enterprises, NGOs, and citizens. With this trend, policy change and governance have become the new 'buzzwords'. Initiatives for policy change and new governance arrangements can stem both from the grass-roots level (bottom up), and from public authorities (top-down). In this course, students learn and apply key theories about how policy change takes place in a dynamic governance context. In so doing, special attention is drawn to theories covering the various stages of the policy process: problem definition, agenda setting, decision making, implementation, and evaluation. The course covers full working days. Each day consists of three parts: lectures (except for Fridays), group work in tutorials, and independent self-study. During the course, students use the theoretical insights from the literature and the lectures to conduct an in-depth analysis of a specific policy change trajectory in one of the following domains: agriculture, water management, nature conservation and forest management. The analyses are performed in small groups in the afternoons. The four specific policy change trajectories that students can choose from are (i) the EU Common Agricultural Policy, (ii) Room for the River (Ruimte voor de Rivier), (iii) nature conservation in the Oostvaardersplassen, and (iv) forest fires in California, USA. The group work consists of three weekly assignments, which make up fifty (50) percent of the total grade for the course. The course ends with an exam that aids in assessing the students’ understanding of the basic concepts and theoretical perspectives that are discussed in the lectures and literature. The course is part of the governance track of the Bachelor program Economie en Beleid (BEB; Economics and Governance) and builds on the introductory courses ‘Public Administration and Policy Making’ and ‘Environmental Economics and Environmental Policy’ in year 1. It aims at enhancing the students’ ability to grasp and apply key theoretical public policy and governance concepts and perspectives. Beside BEB students, the course is also relevant for BSc. and MSc. students from other disciplines who have an interest in public policy and governance and/or follow a track at the Public Administration and Policy Group (PAP).
descriptions.AC: - lectures; - reading literature and independent study; - analyzing a policy change trajectory in small groups; - providing feedback on the work of other groups.
descriptions.LT: Knill, C. & Tosun, J. (2020). Public Policy: A New Introduction (2nd Ed.). Basingstoke: Pallgrave Macmillan.

objectives: Explain theories related to the different stages of the policy cycle
Explain the governance context in which processes of policy change take place
Analyse a specific policy change trajectory by applying governance and public policy theories
Evaluate and critically reflect on patterns of policy change

RHI10806.name: Economics and Governance in Historical Perspective

descriptions.CO: This introductory course for the program Economics and Governance familiarizes students with the interplay of market forces and government policies in processes of economic growth and the distribution of wealth and income. The course consists of three parts. First, students are introduced to the topic of economic inequality in a global and long-run perspective. Through course materials, lectures and assignments, students are provided with tools to measure and explain income and wealth inequality within and between countries. The second part of the course focuses on market failure and the opportunities for government intervention in the economy. Students discuss concrete economic policy proposals and instruments in the field of the environment, nutrition and agriculture. The relationship between national, European and global governance will be analyzed in more detail. The third part of the course is an introduction into information literacy. Students learn how to use the Wageningen digital environment, the Wageningen library, the proper application of academic referencing systems and the use of MS Excel for quantitative data collection and analysis.
descriptions.AC: - lectures; - literature study and tutorials; - it is expected that students will prepare the relevant literature for the lectures and that they participate actively in the discussions; - students also have to write and present a (group) paper.
descriptions.LT: Milanovic, B. (2016). Global inequality: a new approach for the age of globalization. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press. Several addtitional journal articles. Literature for papers. A course guide can be found on the Brightspace of this course.

objectives: Outline the key dimensions and drivers of economic inequality within and between countries, in a global and long-run perspective
Appreciate the benefits and limitations of measuring economic outcomes such as national income or inequality
Name and critically reflect upon economic governance instruments in the field of the environment, nutrition and agriculture
Use the theoretical insights and empirical examples provided in the course materials, lectures and assignments to reflect on the interplay between market forces and government policies
Use the Wageningen digital environment, including the collection of literature for course assignments
Memorize and apply the rules for proper scientific referencing
Show a basic understanding of the functionalities of MS Excel for quantitative data collection and analysis
Apply the basic skills of structuring and writing an academic paper

RHI30806.name: The Origins of Global Economic Inequality

descriptions.AK: Some basic knowledge of economic theory and quantitative analyses.
descriptions.CC: This course may be taken by BEB or BIN students considering writing their BSc-thesis at RHI.
descriptions.CO: Why have some countries grown rich while others have remained poor? Why did the ‘West’ industrialize first? What explains the Asian ‘renaissance’? Why is Latin America caught in a middle-income trap? And will Africa be growing out of poverty in the 21st Century? A deeper understanding of these topics is crucial to make progress on various Sustainable Development Goals, including the worldwide eradication of poverty. Since countries don’t grow rich in a just few years’ time, and poverty doesn’t disappear overnight, answering these big questions requires a long-term perspective. Indeed, the ‘great divergence’ in economic performance and living standards across countries and world regions has a history stretching back for centuries. Economic historians have collected impressive amounts of data to study these divergent experiences. Systematic comparative analyses of historical data has enhanced explanatory models of growth and inequality. In this course we examine the roots of global economic inequality include the role of geography and disease, natural resources, trade, technology, political and social systems, and legal, financial, and commercial institutions. We review the historical evidence on the origins of global economic inequality and links the evidence to a range of economic theories explaining (parts of) the great divergence in income and wealth after 1500.
descriptions.AC: - lectures; - tutorials; - self-study.
descriptions.LT: Mark Koyama and Jared Rubin (2022). How the World Became Rich: The Historical Origins of Economic Growth. Cambridge, UK: Polity Press. Articles and chapters to be announced in the course manual.

objectives: Summarise the key facts about the origins and development of global economic inequality
Explain the fundamental causes of the British industrial Revolution and subsequent patterns of global technology diffusion and connect these to growing income disparities until today
Explain why long-term perspectives are crucial to assess progress on various Sustainable Development Goals, and the poverty eradication goal in particular
Find and apply longitudinal data to formulate and investigate original research questions on long-term economic development and global inequality in written assignments
Analyse the link between global income inequality and the long-run development of living standards, including health and education
Evaluate the different positions in academic debates on the drivers of global economic inequality

Evaluate the benefits and limitations of specific theories on long-term growth and inequality (e.g. international trade theory, factor-biased technological change, institutional theory, politcial economy and public choice)

UEC22806.name: Spatial and Regional Economics

descriptions.AK: DEC10306 Economics or UEC10406 Microeconomics and Behaviour
descriptions.CO: Economic activities take place within geographical space. At the essence of spatial and regional economics is that location and distance matter, resulting in interactions in space that can influence various forms of economic activity. For example, firms can change their location and input demand and output supply decisions depending on market conditions and the distance to the relevant input and output markets. Similarly, households can decide on location, consumption and labor supply also depending on spatial factors. Thus, space and its characteristics can influence the choices agents make. What is the best location to start a business? To buy a house? To follow education? To join the labor market? The answer strongly depends on the (expected) costs and benefits of a certain location, as well as the costs and benefits in other locations. Certain places seem to be advantageous to many firms and households and hence, clustering of economic activities takes place. In this course we focus on two aspects of spatial and regional economics: location theory and regional development. Location theory deals with location choices of firms and households and the resulting land use. We first start off by examining the behavior of individual firms from a theoretical perspective. This is extended to groups of firms, resulting in agglomeration economies and clustering phenomena. We then look further into the spatial distribution of activities, land use and land markets. This also provides a backbone for analyzing cities and urban-rural interactions. We then extend the analysis to examine regional specialization, trade and multiplier linkages operating between different sectors and regions. The regional development part focuses on socioeconomic differences within and between regions in both developed and developing countries. We first look into regional and interregional labor market analysis, including the role labor migration plays in the economic adjustment processes of regions. This will include an appraisal of theoretical and empirical insights on regional unemployment disparities. As factor allocation mechanisms across space can influence economic growth, we discuss the nature of regional growth including Keynesian perspectives. Then, regional inequality and policy, as well as wellbeing will be covered. Finally, there will be a discussion on regional voting patterns. Through a combination of lectures, practicals, excursion, group report and presentation, you will gain knowledge on spatial and regional economic concepts, theories and policy. In addition, you will acquire experience using spatial data, empirical methods and interpreting results.
descriptions.AC: - attending lectures; - compulsory attendance of practical sessions and excursion; - group assignment and presentation.
descriptions.LT: McCann, P. (2013) Modern Urban and Regional Economics, 2nd edition, Oxford University Press. Additional information on material will be made available in Brightspace.

objectives: Reproduce spatial and regional economic theories and concepts
Solve and interpret applications of location and regional development concepts and theories
Apply these concepts to spatial and regional socioeconomic phenomena and policy options
Analyse socioeconomic and policy options using spatial and regional economic approaches

UEC23306.name: Pluralist Economics for Sustainable Food Systems

descriptions.AK: DEC10306 (Economics)
descriptions.CO: The global food system is associated with various issues of sustainability and social justice, from mangrove deforestation in aquaculture, to worker conditions in horticulture, to food deserts in cities. All these issues are about economics – how to organise the food system to meet consumer demands – but they also raise very diverse questions on ethics, power, and environmental sustainability. This diversity of questions and issues requires a similar diversity of perspectives on economics. This course introduces students to a variety of perspectives on economics, or schools of thought, and discusses their strengths, their weaknesses, and what insights they can give us into the various problems with the food production system. What does Marxist economics have to say about worker conditions in horticulture? How does the view of environmental economists on circular agriculture compare to that of ecological economists? What can we learn from behavioural economics about obesity?
descriptions.AC: Each week is devoted to a specific theme related to the global food system. This theme is discussed from different economic perspectives in two lectures and one tutorial that takes the form of a debate. Students prepare for the debate by collecting arguments in a group, drawing from the relevant economic schools of thought and other sources.

objectives: Explain the core elements of various schools of thought in economics
Apply various economic schools of thought to current issues in the food system
Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of various economic schools of thought
Formulate, evaluate, and communicate arguments in writing and debate
Integrate various perspectives in an analysis of a current issue in the food system

UEC31806.name: Economics and Governance of Energy Transitions

descriptions.AK: AEP21306 Econometrics ENR20306 Environmental Economics and Environmental Policy UEC10406 Microeconomics and Behaviour UEC21806 Microeconomics PAP30806 Governance and Policy Change
descriptions.CO: The transition towards sustainable energy is complex and contested. It involves issues related to international markets, environmental externalities and social and spatial inequalities, and it comes with high economic costs and concerns from diverse stakeholders. While the urgency of transitions is widely acknowledged, there are important decisions to be made: who should take action, which processes and instruments fit best, and how to evaluate policy interventions. What is clear is that the current debate requires well-informed integrated economic and governance insights. In this course students capitalize on what they have learned in the first two years of the BEB programme and apply their knowledge, methods and skills to problems of energy transitions in the Netherlands, Europe and elsewhere. Questions that will be explored include: Why do we need an energy transition? What do energy markets currently look like? What market failures prevail? How can we reach acceleration, and facilitate that small scale policy decisions accumulate to large-scale change? What is the stakeholder force field both nationally and internationally? Who is included and excluded in decision-making – and how to come to fair and just policies? What are trade-offs between agglomeration economies and network constraints? Should we account for urban and rural differences? What are the trade-offs between short- and long-term goals, and how we can measure this? What are the main policy controversies and how do they influence the transition? What is the potential for policy interventions?
descriptions.AC: The course includes lectures, tutorials, group assignments, and an individual report. During the lectures we discuss several issues and theories regarding energy transitions, at several scales, from economics and governance perspectives. During the tutorials the students will work in groups on assignments in which they apply quantitative and qualitative research methods to analyze these issues. The assignments will be graded. The individual report is an in-depth policy report for a region on approaching a specific aspect of the energy transition, and should integrate the economics and governance perspectives. The final version of the individual report will be submitted at the end of the period. As such, this course will also be a good preparation for the Bachelor thesis.
descriptions.LT: To be announced.
descriptions.RES: Resit information for the assignments is given in the Examination paragraph.

objectives: Apply advanced economic and governance theories to energy transitions
Collect, analyse and interpret relevant information (such as policy documents and data) in the field of economics and governance related to energy transitions
Apply qualitative and quantitative economic and governance analysis methods to energy transitions
Design and evaluate potential policy interventions to stimulate the energy transition for a specific region
Reflect on the usefulness of integrating economic and governance theories

YRM10306.name: Research Methods in the Social Sciences

descriptions.CO: The goal of the course is that students learn to develop a research proposal for a fundamental or practical scientific research project. Starting from a practical problem that needs to be solved, the student first learns to design an appropriate research objective and appropriate research questions. Then students learn to set up the research project according to the following research designs: the experiment, the cross-sectional design, and the case study. By the end of the course students will be able to hand in a complete, detailed and feasible research proposal.
descriptions.AC: - lectures; - tutorials; - home assignments; - studying of literature.
descriptions.LT: Scheepers, P.L.H., & Tobi, H. (2021). Onderzoeksmethoden (tiende druk). Amsterdam: Boom. ISBN 9789024438082.

objectives: Recognise and apply the empirical and regulative cycles
Develop a conceptual research design, formulate an adequate research objective, derive a set of research questions, operationalise multi-dimensional concepts
Recognise and develop a technical research design (experimental, cross-sectional, longitudinal, case-study), formulate hypotheses, generate a plan for data analysis
Recognise and describe data-collection methods suitable for social science research
Apply the methods for random and non-random sampling
Explain and apply the methodological concepts of reliability and validity (measurement, internal, external)
Critically assess one's own research design and research designs from others

YSS10906.name: Analysis of a Problem Situation

descriptions.AK: This course makes use of the knowledge acquired in the first year courses in P1 to P5 of the respective programmes: BBC, BEB, and BIN.
descriptions.CO: This course follows the so-called 'problem-oriented' method which means that students are required to apply the knowledge they have acquired previously on a complex societal problem. To this end, students first make a choice between seven themes. Once a theme is chosen students (in a group) write a proposal to analyse the problem at hand, emphasising ethical aspects. On the basis of this proposal students carry out a (desk) study based on literature and/or interviews and present a final report (both orally and written) of their findings. An important characteristic of the groups is that these are composed of students coming from various disciplines so as to ensure a multi-disciplinary approach.
descriptions.AC: - introductory lectures to the themes; - introductory assignments; - determination of a research subject and development of a research proposal; - carry out the proposed research; - writing the scientific research report; - presentation of the research.
descriptions.LT: Start-up literature is available at the beginning of the course, final literature depends on the theme and the research proposal.
descriptions.RES: If the report is insufficient, the group can make an agreement with the supervising lecturer about when to deliver an improved version of the report.

objectives: Identify and describe complex societal problems using relevant social science perspectives and formulate a focused and researchable questions
Design a well-structured research proposal that applies appropriate theories and methods from the social sciences, addressing relevant ethical considerations
Collect and interpret qualitative and quantitative data following a clear research plan, demonstrating understanding of research quality and reliability
Apply relevant social science theories and analytical tools to explain findings and situate results within broader societal debates
Communicate research findings effectively in written and oral formats, presenting evidence-based conclusions and recommendations
Collaborate effectively in diverse, multidisciplinary teams by respecting different perspectives, providing constructive feedback and developing skills for societal change

YSS81312.name: BSc Thesis Economics and Governance

descriptions.AK: See: Course guide BSc Thesis BEB.
descriptions.CO: The course consists of the Bachelor Assessment (1 credit) and the thesis report (11 credits) . Students are only allowed to start with their thesis writing after the successful completion of the Assessment part. a) The assessment assists students in developing a clear view on their personality, characteristics and potential. Using the outcomes of an aptitude test students start thinking about their career in an early stage of the academic program. This will strengthen their ability to make proper choices in study programs and focus from year 3 on. They will visit an alumnus working in their field of interest for a reality 'check'. Students discuss, based on acquired insights, a well explained study plan with the study advisor. b) The BSc thesis The BSc thesis can be written under supervision of the staff of the chair groups: AEP, DEC, ENP, ENR, PAP, RHI, or UEC. The student has to study (by means of a literature review or empirical research) a subject within the field of the major and prove to have sufficient knowledge to critically analyse and summarize the given subject. He/she must also be able to clearly communicate the findings in writing and by oral presentation. The subject will be determined in consultation with the thesis supervisor. The student has to define the research problem and formulate research questions in a proper way, deal with the logistics of carrying out such an individual research project, plan and schedule the different activities in a decent way, and present the results in writing in a clearly organized report.
descriptions.AC: The Bachelor Assessment, which includes an aptitude test, two meetings with your study advisor, and a report including an interview with an alumnus and the motivated choice for a Master programme. The BSc thesis, which includes conducting a (literature) study, writing, presenting and orally defending a research report.
descriptions.LT: To be accorded with the supervisor.

objectives: BSc assessment LO1: Interpret own competencies and motives
BSc assessment LO2: Design and plan own study learning processes based on reflection upon personal knowledge, skills, attitudes and performance
Formulate a research problem and do (literature) research according to scientific standards
Integrate knowledge from various sources and apply theoretical knowledge obtained in the study
Work individually and independently in scientific research (under supervision)
Plan and carry out work within the available time
Report in writing in a clear and understandable way
Orally present and defend the results of such work

ZSS06000.name: General Safety

descriptions.CO: At WUR we value your safety. Therefore many measures are taken in order to facilitate a safe study in Wageningen. And although all these measures are in place still one of the most important factors for a safe stay is YOUR behavior and knowledge of these measures. Therefore the General Safety course is mandatory for all new students at WUR. This course will introduce you to safety at Wageningen University & Research. We'll cover a broad range of topics to prepare you for a safe stay at our university: in case of emergency: how to respond to emergencies; computer work: how to prevent complaints on arms, neck and shoulder (CANS/ RSI); social safety and being an active bystander.
descriptions.AC: E-learning modules

objectives: Have a basic understanding on how safety is managed at WUR
Know the difference between risks and hazards
Report accidents and incidents
Know which general rules apply regarding safety at WUR
Know which factors contribute to an ergonomic workspace
Adjust the computer workspace to work ergonomically correct
Know how to act as an active bystander
Know how to give and ask for consent in social engagements
Know where to seek help

ZSS06200.name: Fieldwork Safety

descriptions.CO: At WUR we value your safety. Going into the field for an excursion or for observations/ measurements exposes you to specific risks some of which you'd take for granted while visiting nature or urban environments outside the university perspective. Things like traffic or uneven terrain seems something that you face on a day to day basis, but need a more strict approach while facing them in a professional way. Furthermore infection prevention and social responsible behavior are topics that require specific attention. Therefore many measures are taken in order to facilitate a safe study in Wageningen. And although all these measures are in place still one of the most important factors for a safe stay is YOUR behavior and knowledge of these measures. Therefore the Fieldwork Safety course is mandatory for all students going into the field for their education. This course will introduce you to safe fieldwork during courses at WUR and will cover a range of topics: how to prepare for fieldwork; what risk can you be exposed to when working in the field.
descriptions.AC: E-learning modules

objectives: Know which basic safety rules apply to fieldwork
Know how to prepare for the safety risks in fieldwork
Know some basic risks that apply to working in the field
